title: Akal Ustat
hook: praise of the Timeless One in many meters

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Dasam Granth, the book of the Tenth, and how Sikhs talk about its make-up. Your line was discussed with respect. Whose side did you put into fair words? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

A marching drum. Then a lullaby. Then a fast, tumbling chant, the kind that makes your tongue work. Then something slow enough to walk to. If a single poem changed its rhythm that often, you'd expect it to change its subject too. This one doesn't. Every beat, every speed, points at the same One. It sits inside the Dasam Granth, and Sikhs pray parts of it in the morning. Its name is a description of what it does.
screen: `A DRUM, A LULLABY, A CHANT.` → `ONE SUBJECT THROUGH IT ALL.` → `A NAME THAT SAYS WHAT IT DOES.`

segments.voice: Akal Ustat: praise of the Timeless One. Akal is the One beyond time, the One that death and change don't reach. Ustat is praise. And the poem moves through many meters, many verse forms, as if every rhythm in the poet's ear had to take a turn. It opens with a line of shelter, given here in paraphrase: the Timeless Being is my protector; the All-Steel is my protector. All-Steel, Sarab Loh, is a name for God that sounds like a blade, the strength that doesn't bend. So the first thing praise does here is lean. Before it says anything grand, it says: I'm held. Then come the stanzas recited in the Sikh morning prayers, the swayyas called Tav Prasad. Their pattern is a long parade. In paraphrase: I have seen the pure and the holy men, ascetics and yogis. I have seen mighty kings with elephants and banners, armies stretching away. I have seen pilgrims bathing at sacred places. And then the turn that comes back again and again: without the love of the Lord, without His grace, all of it counts for nothing. One stanza ends with a line tradition holds dear, again in paraphrase: I speak the truth, all of you, listen; only those who loved have found the Lord. That's the engine of the whole poem. It doesn't mock kings or pilgrims. It walks past them with open eyes and says that the Timeless One is reached by love, not by size. Praise, in Akal Ustat, isn't flattery. It's a way of putting things back in their right scale: the armies are small, and the One is not.
screen: `PRAISE OF THE TIMELESS ONE.` · `THE ALL-STEEL IS MY PROTECTOR.` · `KINGS, YOGIS, PILGRIMS PASS BY.` · `ONLY THOSE WHO LOVED FOUND THE LORD.` · then, large: `PRAISE OF THE TIMELESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: listen to a stanza. Settle, and breathe. If you can, find a recording of the Tav Prasad swayyas and let one play, even if you don't follow the words. Listen for the rhythm more than the meaning. If you can't play one now, just let the parade pass in your mind: the kings, the armies, the pilgrims. Let each one go by. Then let the last line arrive, only those who loved, and stay with it. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Akal Ustat. Praise of the Timeless One, in many meters: the poem that walks past kings and pilgrims and says the Lord is found by love. Today's word.
Your line: praise of the timeless. Today, when something big impresses you, a car, a title, a crowd, put it back in scale. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Tav Prasad swayyas from Akal Ustat as part of their morning prayers, and stanzas of Akal Ustat are sung as kirtan in gurdwaras.
